a: Earth's Moon is 3,475 km across, about a quarter of Earth's width, and orbits about 384,400 km away. It takes 27.3 days to orbit, and keeps the same face towards us. 12 astronauts walked on it (Apollo, 1969-1972).
s: NASA Science moon pages / NSSDCA Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters (JPL SSD)

a: Phobos is Mars's bigger moon, a lumpy rock about 22 km across. It's slowly spiralling inwards and will break up or crash into Mars in about 50 million years.
s: NASA Science moon pages / NSSDCA Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters (JPL SSD)

a: Deimos is Mars's smaller moon, about 12 km across. It orbits once every 30 hours.
s: NASA Science moon pages / NSSDCA Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters (JPL SSD)

a: Io (Jupiter) is the most volcanically active world in the Solar System, with hundreds of volcanoes, some shooting lava fountains tens of km high. It's 3,643 km across.
s: NASA Science moon pages / NSSDCA Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters (JPL SSD)

a: Europa (Jupiter) is 3,122 km across, a bit smaller than our Moon, with an icy shell over a salty ocean that may hold twice as much water as Earth's oceans. NASA's Europa Clipper launched in October 2024 to study it.
s: NASA Science moon pages / NSSDCA Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters (JPL SSD)

a: Callisto (Jupiter) is 4,821 km across and one of the most heavily cratered surfaces in the Solar System.

a: Titan (Saturn) is 5,150 km across, the second-biggest moon. It has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. NASA's Dragonfly drone is due to launch in 2028.

a: Charon is Pluto's biggest moon, 1,212 km across, about half Pluto's size. Pluto and Charon always show each other the same face.

a: Eris is a dwarf planet about 2,326 km across, almost exactly Pluto's size but about 27% more massive. Its discovery in 2005 led the IAU to define 'planet' in 2006.
s: NASA Science: Eris; IAU Resolution B5 (2006)

a: Haumea is an egg-shaped dwarf planet beyond Neptune that spins once every 3.9 hours, one of the fastest-spinning big objects known. It even has a ring.
s: NASA Science: Haumea; Ortiz et al. 2017, Nature

a: Makemake is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, about 1,430 km across, discovered in 2005.
s: NASA Science: Makemake

k: why is pluto not a planet
a: The IAU (2006) says a planet orbits the Sun, is round, and has cleared its orbit of other stuff. Dwarf planets like Pluto, Eris, Ceres, Haumea and Makemake are round but haven't cleared their orbits. The IAU recognises 5 dwarf planets.
s: IAU Resolution B5 and B6 (2006)

a: The main asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. Despite the movies, it's mostly empty space: all of it together has only about 3% of the Moon's mass, and Ceres holds about a quarter of that.
s: NASA Science: Asteroids

a: The Kuiper Belt is a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, from about 30 to 50 AU from the Sun. Pluto, Haumea and Makemake live there.
s: NASA Science: Kuiper Belt

a: The Oort Cloud is a vast, thought-to-exist shell of icy objects, maybe 2,000 to 100,000 AU from the Sun. Nobody has seen it directly yet; long-period comets hint it's there.
s: NASA Science: Oort Cloud

a: Comets are dirty snowballs of ice and dust. Near the Sun they grow glowing tails that point away from it. Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years; next in 2061.
s: NASA Science: Comets

a: The Solar System has the Sun, 8 planets, at least 5 dwarf planets, hundreds of moons, and millions of asteroids and comets. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago. (On this map the planets are drawn bigger than real so you can see them.)
s: NASA Science: Solar System; IAU

a: Voyager 1 (launched 1977) is the farthest human-made object, now well over 160 AU from the Sun. It crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Its light-speed signals take over 22 hours to reach us.

a: 1 AU is the average Earth-Sun distance, fixed by the IAU (2012) at exactly 149,597,870,700 metres (about 150 million km), or about 8.3 light-minutes.

a: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in Orion, very roughly 550 light-years away (distance estimates vary widely). If it sat where the Sun is, it would reach past Mars, maybe beyond. It will explode as a supernova some time in the next 100,000 years or so.
s: NASA Science; Joyce et al. 2020, ApJ 902, 63

a: Polaris, the North Star, sits almost exactly above Earth's north pole, so it hardly moves in the sky. It's a supergiant about 430 light-years away.

a: A star is a giant ball of hot gas powered by nuclear fusion in its core. The Milky Way alone has roughly 100 to 400 billion of them. Red dwarfs, small cool stars, are the most common kind.
s: NASA Science: Stars

a: Red dwarfs are small, cool stars (under about half the Sun's mass). They're about three quarters of all stars, and can shine for trillions of years. Proxima Centauri and TRAPPIST-1 are red dwarfs.
s: NASA Science; RECONS

a: A black hole is where gravity is so strong that not even light escapes. The Milky Way's central one, Sagittarius A*, has about 4 million times the Sun's mass; the Event Horizon Telescope imaged it in 2022. M87's is about 6.5 billion Suns (imaged 2019).
s: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2019, 2022 (ApJL)

a: A supernova is a star exploding: for a few weeks it can outshine a whole galaxy. They make and scatter elements like iron, so you're partly made of exploded-star dust.
s: NASA Science: Supernovae

a: When a Sun-like star dies it leaves a white dwarf: about Earth-sized but with roughly half the Sun's mass. Heavier stars can leave neutron stars, about 20 km across, and pulsars are spinning neutron stars.
s: NASA Science: Star lifecycle

a: Voids are huge, nearly empty bubbles between the walls and filaments of the cosmic web, typically tens to hundreds of millions of light-years across. They fill most of the universe's volume.

a: On the biggest scales galaxies form a cosmic web: clusters at the knots, filaments and walls between them, and giant voids in the gaps. Dark matter's gravity built it from tiny ripples in the early universe. Every dot on this map is a real galaxy tracing it.

a: A light-year is a distance, not a time: how far light travels in a year, about 9.46 trillion km. Light from the Moon takes 1.3 seconds, from the Sun 8 minutes 20 seconds.
A parsec (pc) is 3.26 light-years: the distance at which a star shifts by 1 arcsecond as Earth goes round the Sun. Astronomers love it. 1 kpc = 1,000 pc; 1 Mpc = 1 million pc.
s: IAU Resolution B2 (2015)

a: 1 megaparsec (Mpc) is 1 million parsecs, or 3.26 million light-years, about 3.1 × 10^19 km. This map's distances are in Mpc.

a: Redshift (z) is how much a galaxy's light has been stretched to redder wavelengths by the expansion of the universe. Bigger z means farther away and further back in time; z = 0.1 is about 1.4 billion light-years. This map turns redshifts into 3D positions.
s: Hubble 1929; Planck 2018 cosmology (as used on this map)

a: The universe is expanding: the farther a galaxy, the faster it moves away (Hubble's law). The rate, the Hubble constant, is about 67-73 km/s per megaparsec. Different methods disagree slightly, which is called the 'Hubble tension'.
s: Planck 2018 (67.4); Riess et al. 2022 (73.0)

a: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old (13.787 ± 0.020 billion, Planck 2018). The most distant galaxies on this map are seen as they were about 9.6 billion years ago.

a: The Big Bang wasn't an explosion in space: it was space itself starting hot and dense and expanding everywhere at once, about 13.8 billion years ago.
s: NASA WMAP; Planck 2018

a: The cosmic microwave background is the Big Bang's afterglow, released about 380,000 years after it began, when the universe cooled enough to turn see-through. Today it's a cold 2.725 K glow from every direction.

a: Dark matter is invisible stuff that doesn't shine or absorb light but has gravity. There's about five times more of it than normal matter. We see its pull on galaxies and clusters (Zwicky 1933, Rubin 1970s), but nobody knows what it is yet.
s: Planck 2018 (~27% of the universe); Rubin & Ford 1970

a: Dark energy is the mystery making the universe's expansion speed up, discovered in 1998 with supernovae (Nobel Prize 2011). It's about 68% of the universe's energy. DESI's 2024-2025 results hint it might change over time.
